extracted.subtask_description: An exploratory research article reporting interviews with research mathematicians about the goals that guide their reading of published proofs and the types of reasoning they use; identifies three general reading strategies and discusses the role of non-deductive reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appealing to the authority of other mathematicians who read the proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Appealing to the authority of other mathematicians who read the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reading strategy in which a reader relies on the judgment or endorsement of other mathematicians (testimony/authority) about a proof rather than verifying every detail themselves. This can speed acceptance but depends on trust in others' competence and consensus; related empirical work (e.g., Inglis & Mejia-Ramos, 2009) examines the effect of authority on persuasiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line-by-line reading
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reading strategy involving detailed, sequential checking of each inferential step in a proof. This approach aims at local verification of correctness (stepwise validation) and is the most thorough form of checking, but is time-consuming and may be used when absolute certainty or learning of fine details is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modular reading
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strategy that treats a proof as composed of modules (lemmas, claims, or components) and evaluates those larger units rather than every single step. Readers check the structure and connections between modules, relying on higher-level plausibility and the correctness of component results to form an overall judgment more efficiently than line-by-line checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals guiding reading of published proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: The goals guiding their reading of published proofs (as reported by interviewed mathematicians).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study investigates what objectives (e.g., validation, understanding, extracting methods, or application) drive mathematicians' choices of reading strategy. Different goals motivate different balances between thoroughness, efficiency, and reliance on authority or non-deductive reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-deductive reasoning plays an important role
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-deductive reasoning plays an important role in each of these three strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Across appealing-to-authority, line-by-line, and modular strategies, mathematicians use non-deductive reasoning (heuristics, plausibility, analogy, testimonial trust) to reach their goals rather than purely formal deductive checking. The article argues for acknowledging and characterizing these non-deductive elements in studies of proof reading and validation.
